author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Edge of the Storm
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The shore gate passed the first inspection and failed the second.

Danse stared at the measurement as if the number had insulted him personally.

Toph stood beside the retaining wall with one hand resting against the stone.

"Told you," she said.

"You told me it was moving," Danse answered. "You didn't tell me how much."

"I can't see your little ruler from here."

"You don't need to see it. You need to give me a repeatable observation."

I looked at the tide chart.

A storm was moving toward Tideglass. The old service passage beneath the cove remained sealed, but pressure readings at the lower gate had changed. The engineers had agreed to inspect the upper shore gate before the next heavy tide. It was the safest route for moving supplies away from the water, and the hinge had been repaired after the last flood.

The first measurement showed it opening freely.

The second, taken after the stone support had been dampened, showed the gate dragging against its frame.

The difference was small.

It was enough.

"Can we use it tonight?" I asked.

Danse looked at the figures.

"Not under full load."

Toph placed her palm against the support.

"The stone's shifting when the hinge takes weight. I can feel the pressure move through the wall."

Danse shook his head.

"The displacement is within the margin for an unloaded gate."

"That's not the same as safe," Toph said.

I felt the old temptation to pick whichever answer sounded more certain. Danse had calculations. Toph had experience that didn't fit neatly on the page. Both were trying to protect people.

Fen arrived with the updated tide prediction.

"The strongest surge will reach the lower landing after dark," they said. "We need a route for the families by the cove."

"Then we close the gate and use the ridge path," I said.

Tamsin looked up from the hinge.

"The ridge is longer."

"I know."

"Some people will need assistance."

"Then we ask what they need and arrange it."

Danse looked at me.

"You're making a decision before the test is complete."

"I'm deciding not to use an uncertain route during a storm. We can finish the test without putting people through it."

He considered that.

Then he nodded.

"That's defensible."

Toph grinned.

"Look at that. The numbers and the dirt both agree."

I almost laughed.

The work didn't end there.

We had to tell people the gate was closed, not merely hang a sign at a height half the village couldn't see. Pip wrote the notice. Edda checked the upper route for turning space and places to rest. Greg offered to carry lanterns but not to work past his agreed shift. Mara packed food for anyone who might need to wait at the hall.

Maui watched the preparations, his hook resting against his shoulder.

"I can carry people over the wall," he said.

"If somebody asks and it's safe," I answered.

He nodded.

"Right."

The storm arrived early.

Rain moved across the cove in sheets. The sea turned the color of iron. I helped Fen check the last marker by the signal post, then returned along the upper path as the wind grew strong enough to push at my coat.

At the hall, people were arriving in small groups. Some had chosen to leave their homes temporarily. Others stayed where the buildings were safe. We did not force anyone through a Threadway, and nobody had to explain why they preferred a particular place to wait.

The lanterns flickered.

A child began to cry.

Maui crouched beside her and asked whether she wanted a story. She nodded. He told her about a crab so vain it demanded a crown from the moon.

She laughed through her tears.

The lights went out halfway through the ending.

For a second the room was entirely dark.

Then someone lit a hand lantern near the door. Another light appeared by the kitchen. Danse sent a message from Brasswatch: the generator had failed under the surge, but backup lamps were available and repairs were underway.

We counted people without making a public list of private destinations.

Everyone in the hall was accounted for.

The hall went quiet after the bell. Fen kept their hand on the tide chart, waiting for the signal to end. The note faded slowly, like a cup humming after someone had touched the rim.

A child asked whether the sound meant the lower gate was opening.

"No," Fen said. "We don't have evidence of that. The old passage remains sealed. The pressure may be changing at a different point."

The answer was less exciting than a story about a door beneath the ocean. It also let everyone stay where they were instead of running toward a tunnel nobody had authorized them to enter.

A volunteer brought in a fresh lantern and checked the path to the shelter entrance. The first sign had slipped in the wind. Edda pointed out that the replacement blocked the handrail when someone held it upright.

"Shift it left," she said. "There. Now it gives directions without becoming another obstacle."

We moved two crates from the hallway. The pantry workers had already set aside food for the overnight watch, and the blankets Maui was carrying came from a labeled shelf that would need replenishing when the storm ended.

I wanted to go outside and see what the waves were doing. I also knew that my wanting to witness danger didn't make me useful to the people around me.

"Could I help with the head count?" I asked Neri.

"Yes. But use the private check-in sheet. We don't post people's destinations."

Maui watched the process, blankets held carefully against his chest.

"All this work before anything happens," he said.

"That's how we give people choices if something does," Neri answered.

He looked at me over the last bundle. "I suppose tearing the gate apart would be quicker."

"Quickly worse, maybe."

He laughed, then turned to help a visitor find the warm room. When he came back, he took my hand for one moment, not to claim my attention but to ask whether I was all right.

"I am," I said. "I'm frightened, but I'm here."

"So am I."

For once that was the whole heroic speech. The next bell did not sound. We stayed until the watches were assigned and the lanterns were checked again.

Outside, the second bell sounded.

It came from beneath the sea, deeper than the public bell, and held its note long enough to make the floor tremble. Fen looked toward the windows.

"Pressure change," they said.

"Can we do anything?" I asked.

"Not safely from here."

Maui stood.

I saw the fight move across his face. His instinct was to run toward the sound and tear apart whatever held it.

Then he looked at the children, the lanterns, and the people who had chosen to wait.

"What do you need me to do?" he asked.

Fen handed him a stack of dry blankets.

"Take these to the west bench. Then stay where we can find you."

He did.

The storm passed after midnight. The lower landing was flooded, but the closed shore gate held. Its frame had shifted another fraction under the load, confirming the earlier test. Had we used it heavily, the hinge might have jammed.

No one had to discover that while standing in the doorway.

At dawn, Danse and Toph returned with Tamsin to examine the damage.

Danse crouched beside the gate.

"The wet-load tolerance was inadequate," he said.

Toph tapped the stone.

"That's a polite way of saying it moved."

He looked at her.

"Yes."

She smiled.

"Good. Now let's fix it."

I leaned against the railing, exhausted.

Maui came up beside me with two cups of Iroh's house tea.

"How's the hero business?" I asked.

"Terrible. I carried blankets."

"Very glamorous."

"I also told a crab story."

"That sounds like the important part."

He handed me a cup.

We stood in the cool morning air. The sea was still rough, and the ridge path needed clearing. There would be repairs, funding meetings, and another round of inspection before the gate reopened.

Maui brushed his fingers against mine.

"Do you wish you'd let me break the lower passage open?"

"No."

"Neither do I."

I looked at him.

He was watching the water, not the crowd.

"That surprises you?" he asked.

"A little."

He smiled tiredly.

"I've been paying attention."

I leaned into his shoulder.

The storm hadn't ended the mystery. It had made the evidence more urgent and the repairs more expensive.

We would have to decide what to do next with the people who lived here.

For now, the gate was closed because we had chosen safety over certainty.

That felt like the right kind of courage.
